instructions:
A PDF was filed by hand. Open the file at `attachments.pdf_path` and read it, then produce a structured summary.

Read it as a document, not as text: look at the figures, tables and plots. A result table usually settles what the paper actually achieved faster than the prose does, and a figure often carries the method. If the document is long, read the abstract, introduction, method and results sections in full and skim the rest.

`bibliography` must come from the document itself — its title page, header or footer. The filename is not evidence; it is whatever the person who saved the file happened to type.

`topics` is your judgement. These are the topics this archive tracks; list the slugs this paper genuinely belongs to, and leave the list empty rather than forcing a fit:
- reasoning-evaluation: Reasoning Evaluation — Benchmarks for reasoning and the methodology behind them: what each one actually tests, how contamination and memorization inflate a score, and where a reported gain fails to reproduce. The question the archive answers is which numbers a claim about reasoning can be built on.
- reasoning-faithfulness: Reasoning Faithfulness — The gap between a model's stated chain of thought and the computation that produced its answer: unfaithful or post-hoc rationalization, reasoning that is latent rather than written, encoded or steganographic traces, and what a monitor reading the trace can and cannot catch. The question the archive answers is when a visible reasoning trace is evidence about the model, and when it is only text.
- reasoning-training: Reasoning Training — How a language model acquires long-form reasoning: reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards, process versus outcome supervision, distillation of reasoning traces, and self-training. The question the archive answers is which training signal produces reasoning that generalizes, and what each one costs.
- test-time-scaling: Test-Time Scaling — What a model gains by thinking longer at inference: sampling and verification, search over reasoning steps, self-correction, and the length of the chain itself as a compute knob. The question the archive answers is how accuracy trades against tokens spent, and where that curve flattens.

`relevance` must have one entry per slug you listed in `topics`.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

bibliography.abstract: string - the paper's own abstract, verbatim
bibliography.arxiv_id: string - arXiv id if printed on the document, else empty
authors: string - author name, in the order printed
bibliography.doi: string - DOI if printed on the document, else empty
bibliography.title: string - the paper's own title, exactly as printed
bibliography.venue: string - journal, conference or 'preprint'; empty if unclear
bibliography.year: integer - publication year, 0 if the document does not say

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what
topics: string - slug of a tracked topic this paper belongs to; omit any that do not genuinely apply

payload.title: Step Level Sparse Autoencoder for Reasoning Process Interpretation

bibliography.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong complex reasoning capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, their reasoning patterns remain too complicated to analyze. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpretability, existing approaches predominantly operate at the token level, creating a granularity mismatch when capturing more critical step-level information, such as reasoning direction and semantic transitions. In this work, we propose step-level sparse autoencoder (SSAE), which serves as an analytical tool to disentangle different aspects of LLMs' reasoning steps into sparse features. Specifically, by precisely controlling the sparsity of a step feature conditioned on its context, we form an information bottleneck in step reconstruction, which splits incremental information from background information and disentangles it into several sparsely activated dimensions. Experiments on multiple base models and reasoning tasks show the effectiveness of the extracted features. By linear probing, we can easily predict surface-level information, such as generation length and first token distribution, as well as more complicated properties, such as the correctness and logicality of the step. These observations indicate that LLMs should already at least partly know about these properties during generation, which provides the foundation for the self-verification ability of LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/SSAE
bibliography.title: Step-Level Sparse Autoencoder for Reasoning Process Interpretation
bibliography.venue: ICML 2026 (Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306)

contributions: SSAE, a context-conditioned sparse autoencoder operating on reasoning steps, in which giving the decoder access to the full preceding context forces the sparse code to carry only the step's incremental contribution.

A dynamic sparsity controller that adjusts the L1 weight multiplicatively toward a target sparsity rather than requiring the penalty to be tuned by hand, together with an injected-noise formulation that turns the sparsity target into an explicit information bottleneck.

Probing evidence that step correctness, logical coherence, step length and first-token identity are all decodable from the sparse code by a small MLP, whereas token-level SAE features are near the naive statistical baseline on most of these.

A latent-swap test showing the code is genuinely disentangled from background: decoding a step's code under a different context produces text that does not repeat or paraphrase the original background.

Two downstream uses: N2G pattern mining over feature dimensions, which yields per-model and per-domain profiles of reasoning style, and Probe-Guided decoding, which replaces self-consistency's equal vote with a weight derived from the probed step-correctness probability.
result.limitations: The paper has no limitations section. Several things a reader should weigh. The claim that token-level SAE features are no better than naive baselines is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1 on MATH-500 correctness, where Token-SAE-last and Token-SAE-agg reach 86.79 and 86.88 against a naive 70.65 and actually beat SSAE-Qwen at 82.74; the SSAE advantage is unambiguous for logicality, step length and first-token perplexity, but not for correctness on that benchmark, and the text overstates it. The gains from Probe-Guided decoding over self-consistency are small — between 0.6 and 3.3 points across six model-benchmark pairs — and are shown only on three comparatively easy tasks; the cross-model transfer setting the paper describes, scoring outputs of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on MATH-500 and AIME 2024/2025, is set up in the text but its numbers are not in the main table. Base models are 0.5B and 1B, with larger-model results deferred to an appendix, so the headline interpretability claims rest on small models. Step segmentation is by punctuation and line breaks, a crude proxy for a reasoning step. Out-of-distribution correctness and logicality labels come from GPT-4o-mini and the disentanglement evaluation from a panel of LLM judges, so both the probing targets and the central disentanglement result inherit judge noise, high inter-judge agreement notwithstanding. Finally, the inference from 'correctness is decodable' to 'the model knows' is a probing argument: it establishes that the information is linearly present, not that the model's own generation pathway uses it — a gap the paper itself gestures at when it says models do not know how to leverage this information without post-training calibration.
result.method: A reasoning trajectory is split into steps at natural linguistic boundaries (punctuation, line breaks). For step s_k with context C_k = (s_1..s_{k-1}), a Transformer encoder consumes the concatenation [C_k ; SEP ; s_k] and its final hidden state h_k summarizes the step in relation to its history. A sparse projector expands h_k into a higher-dimensional code via a ReLU layer with sparsity factor c, giving the sparse feature vector. Decoding is also context-conditioned: the code is partitioned into c segments of the model dimension and appended to the embedded context, and the decoder autoregressively reconstructs the step from that combined input. This asymmetry is the central design choice — because the decoder can read the background from C_k directly, the code has no reason to store it, so anything the code does carry is incremental. Training minimizes token-level cross-entropy reconstruction of the step plus an L1 penalty on the code. Rather than tuning the penalty weight, a controller updates it multiplicatively each window according to whether observed sparsity is above or below a target, clipped to a robust range, with step size 0.01. Gaussian noise with sigma 0.01 is added to each code dimension, which together with the sparsity target bounds the information the code can transmit and makes the bottleneck explicit. Two instantiations are trained, initializing encoder and decoder from Qwen2.5-0.5B and from Llama-3.2-1B, with sparsity factor c = 1 and target sparsity 10, on GSM8K-Aug (about 385K samples), NuminaMath-CoT (about 860K) and OpenCodeInstruct. Probing trains a three-layer MLP on the frozen code to predict four step attributes. In-domain labels on GSM8K come from programmatic verification of numerical outputs; out-of-distribution labels on MATH-500 come from GPT-4o-mini acting as a judge. Feature dimensions are mapped to human-readable patterns with Neuron-to-Graph, then labelled and clustered with Gemini-3-Pro. Probe-Guided decoding scores each candidate answer by summing, over 16 sampled steps, the probed correctness probability raised to a temperature exponent; at exponent zero it degenerates to self-consistency, and higher values progressively down-weight paths whose steps the probe judges unreliable.
result.one_liner: Trains a sparse autoencoder over whole reasoning steps rather than tokens, conditioning both encoder and decoder on the preceding trajectory so the sparse code carries only what the step adds, and shows that step correctness, logicality, length and first token are all linearly decodable from that code.
result.problem: Sparse autoencoders are the dominant tool for decomposing model activations into interpretable features, but they operate at the token level, which mismatches the unit reasoning actually happens in. Step-level properties — the direction a step takes, the semantic transition it makes — are not recoverable from a token feature. There is a second, subtler problem the paper identifies: at any step the activation mixes background information already established by earlier steps with the increment the current step contributes, and a token-level SAE entangles the two, so what it recovers is confounded by context the step did not introduce.

relevance.reasoning-faithfulness: The most direct measurement this archive has of the gap between what a model internally represents and what its visible trace acts on. Step correctness is linearly decodable from a step's own sparse code at 78-86% accuracy, meaning the information that a step is wrong is present at the moment the step is produced — and yet the trajectory continues into the error. That is the silent-divergence failure described elsewhere in the archive, now localized to a representation rather than inferred from behaviour, and it sharpens the question this topic asks: the trace is not merely an incomplete report of the computation, it omits something the computation demonstrably has. The paper's own reading, that this is the foundation of self-verification and that models lack the post-training calibration to use it, is a concrete claim about why traces are unfaithful in a specific, fixable way. The disentanglement result matters for method here too: because the code is conditioned on context and verified by latent swap to exclude background, a claim about a step is a claim about that step's contribution rather than about accumulated context, which is the confound that undermines naive probing of reasoning traces.
relevance.test-time-scaling: Probe-Guided decoding is a fourth entry in this archive's pattern of beating self-consistency by weighting trajectories instead of counting them, and it is the only one whose weight comes from an interpretability artefact rather than from output statistics — a probe on internal sparse features rather than entropy, CUSUM statistics or answer-space distances. Its temperature exponent makes the relationship explicit: at zero it is exactly self-consistency, and increasing it progressively discounts paths whose steps the probe distrusts, so the method is a strict generalization of the baseline. The honest caveat for this topic is that the gains are the smallest of the four (0.6-3.3 points at 16 samples on easy benchmarks), and unlike the entropy and CUSUM results there is no sweep showing the margin widening with sample count, which is the evidence this topic has learned to ask for.

result.results: Probing (GSM8K / MATH-500). Step correctness: naive baseline 70.49 / 70.65; Token-SAE-last 72.44 / 86.79; Token-SAE-agg 74.38 / 86.88; SSAE-Qwen 78.58 / 82.74; SSAE-Llama 80.55 / 86.24. Logicality on MATH-500: naive 55.06, Token-SAE-last 60.56, Token-SAE-agg 67.43, SSAE-Qwen 76.56, SSAE-Llama 71.91. The separation is starkest on the two regression targets, where token-level features are at or worse than baseline while SSAE is roughly an order of magnitude better: step length error 28.04 / 33.30 for the baseline and 25.79 / 30.33 for the best token SAE, against 2.10 / 1.94 (SSAE-Qwen) and 2.02 / 1.59 (SSAE-Llama); first-token perplexity 61.01 / 74.96 baseline and 61.55 / 18.63 for the best token SAE, against 4.09 / 1.46 and 2.66 / 1.62. In every case the sparse code beats the dense hidden state it was expanded from, which is the paper's evidence that disentanglement rather than dimensionality is doing the work. Pattern-mining fidelity depends on the sparsity target: at target 10 the N2G F1 is 79.49 (GSM8K), 73.33 (Numina) and 76.20 (OpenCodeInstruct), falling to 61.03 / 56.84 / 47.79 at target 5 and 52.73 / 64.03 / 36.80 at target 3, since a tighter budget forces distinct concepts into one dimension. Feature statistics: 29.01% of dimensions active on average for SSAE-Qwen with Jaccard similarity 0.6716 across steps, versus 15.65% and 0.3052 for SSAE-Llama. The latent-swap test scores 4.91-4.99 out of 5 for semantic independence across GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-pro and DeepSeek-R1 as judges, with observed agreement 94.87-98.75% and Gwet's AC1 0.96-0.99. Pattern profiles differ by domain and by model: code features are dominated by documentation and syntax (over 45% combined), mathematical ones by calculation and derivation (37%) and reasoning (30%); on GSM8K, Llama-3.2-1B devotes 40.4% of features to reasoning against 20% for Qwen2.5-0.5B, which instead concentrates on final resolution. Probe-Guided decoding at 16 samples: Qwen2.5-0.5B reaches 46.80 / 33.00 / 61.67 on GSM8K / SVAMP / MultiArith against self-consistency at 46.20 / 29.67 / 59.44 and single-path averages of 30.40 / 19.33 / 35.56; Llama-3.2-1B reaches 19.40 / 50.33 / 83.89 against 16.60 / 48.00 / 82.78.
